title: The Twelve Huntsmen
paragraphs: A king’s son once had a bride whom he loved dearly. One day, as he sat beside her, perfectly happy, word came that his father was sick and dying and wanted to see him one more time before the end. So he said to his beloved, “I have to go now and leave you. Here is a ring to remember me by. When I am king, I will come back and fetch you.” He rode off, and when he reached his father, the old man was gravely ill and close to death. He said, “Dear son, I wanted to see you once more before I die. Promise me you will marry the woman I choose,” and he named a certain king’s daughter as the intended wife. The son was so distressed that he hardly knew what he was saying. “Yes, dear father,” he answered, “it will be as you wish.” And with that, the king closed his eyes and died.

So after the son had been proclaimed king and the period of mourning was over, he had to keep the promise he had made to his father. He sent to ask for the king’s daughter in marriage, and she was promised to him. His first bride heard about it and grieved so much over his faithlessness that she nearly died. Her father asked her, “Dearest child, why are you so sad? You shall have whatever you want.” She thought for a moment and said, “Dear father, I want eleven girls who look exactly like me, in face, figure, and size.” Her father said, “If it can be done, you shall have your wish.” He had a search made through his whole kingdom, until eleven young women were found who matched his daughter exactly in face, figure, and size.

When they came to the king’s daughter, she had twelve identical huntsmen’s outfits made. The eleven girls had to put on huntsmen’s clothes, and she put on the twelfth suit herself. Then she said goodbye to her father and rode off with them to the court of the man she had once been promised to, whom she still loved so much. She asked whether he needed any huntsmen, and whether he would take all of them into his service. The king looked at her and did not recognize her, but they were such handsome fellows that he said yes, he would gladly take them. And so they became the king’s twelve huntsmen.

Now the king owned a lion, a marvelous animal, for it knew everything hidden and secret. One evening the lion said to the king, “You think you have twelve huntsmen?” “Yes,” said the king, “twelve huntsmen.” The lion went on, “You’re wrong. They are twelve girls.” “That can’t be true,” said the king. “How can you prove it?” “Oh, just have some peas scattered in the antechamber,” answered the lion, “and you’ll soon see. Men have a firm tread, so when they walk over peas, not one of them moves. But girls patter and skip and drag their feet, and the peas roll around.” The king liked the advice and had the peas scattered.

But one of the king’s servants was fond of the huntsmen. When he heard they were about to be tested, he went to them and told them everything. “The lion wants to make the king believe you are girls,” he said. The king’s daughter thanked him and told her girls, “Be strong, and step firmly on the peas.” The next morning, when the king summoned the twelve huntsmen and they entered the antechamber where the peas lay, they stepped so firmly and walked so steadily that not a single pea rolled or moved. After they had gone, the king said to the lion, “You lied to me. They walk just like men.” The lion said, “They were warned about the test, and they made themselves strong. Just have twelve spinning wheels brought into the antechamber. They’ll go over to them and take delight in them, which no man would do.” The king liked this advice too, and had the spinning wheels set up in the antechamber.

But the servant, who was still on the huntsmen’s side, went to them and revealed the plan. When they were alone, the king’s daughter said to her eleven girls, “Hold yourselves back, and don’t look at the spinning wheels.” The next morning, when the king called for his twelve huntsmen, they walked through the antechamber and never once glanced at the spinning wheels. The king said to the lion again, “You have deceived me. They are men, because they didn’t look at the spinning wheels.” The lion answered, “They kept themselves in check.” But the king no longer believed the lion.

The twelve huntsmen always rode behind the king when he went hunting, and his fondness for them kept growing. Then one day, while they were out hunting, word came that the king’s bride was on her way. When the true bride heard this, it hurt her so badly that her heart nearly broke, and she fell to the ground in a faint. The king thought something had happened to his dear huntsman. He ran to him, wanted to help, and pulled off his glove. Then he saw the ring he had given to his first bride, and when he looked into her face, he knew her. His heart was so moved that he kissed her, and when she opened her eyes he said, “You are mine, and I am yours, and nobody in the world can change that.” He sent a messenger to the other bride and begged her to go back to her own kingdom, because he already had a wife, and a man who has just found his old key has no need of a new one. Then the wedding was celebrated, and the lion was taken back into favor, because he had told the truth after all.
